chapter_theme: The Namagal ilampakam opens with the land of Emangadam: the poet calls on learning and fortune, then follows the monsoon from clouds grazing the sea to a flood that carries the mountain's wealth like a generous hand and returns to the sea, and then the ploughing, worshipful sowing and transplanting of the fields, ending on ripened paddy that bows like the learned.

cast.role: the ploughmen and farmers of Emangadam
the field-women who transplant the paddy
the guards who watch the banks in the flood

30.reading: The poet declares that he begins to tell the splendour of the land where the goddess of learning who sits on the tongue and the goddess of fortune who sits on the golden flower embrace a people whose king's learning in song and the arts has travelled across the earth.
30.nuance: The ilampakam takes its name from the first of the two goddesses: learning (the one on the tongue) and fortune (the one on the flower) are set together as the double mark of the land before any of its rivers or fields appear. The run கேள்விக் கோ is compressed; it is read here as the king whose learning by listening is renowned.
30.event: The poet announces that he will describe the land.

31.reading: A ripe coconut falls, tears the honeycomb on the areca's crown, splits a jackfruit, scatters mangoes and knocks down plantains: such is the land whose name, Emangadam, has gone out to every quarter.
31.nuance: Plenty is shown as a chain: one falling fruit sets off four more. The land is named only after the picture of its excess.

32.reading: Flocks of cloud, like the elephant herds of the god who holds the shining discus, graze on the churning clear waves of the sea, flash like the matted hair of the god with the golden konrai, settle on the mountains, climb the sky and roar.
32.nuance: Vishnu's elephants and Siva's lightning-bright locks are used purely as images; the Jain poet takes the two gods as stock similes, with no claim about them. The verse opens a run (32 to 38) that follows the water from the sea, through the mountains and the fields, back to the sea.

33.reading: Massed downpours stand from the honey-laden peaks up to the sky like rows of silver rods, and pour down together.

34.reading: From peaks so high that the horn of the young white moon tears their honeycombs, and that thunder like drums, the white streams of the falls hang like the cloth flags on a crowd of mansions.

35.reading: The falls look like the pearl strings slipped crooked on the chest of crowned Indra, and, since they scatter gold and good gems, like jewel caskets turned upside down.

36.reading: Like the hand of a generous man, the flood takes the rich heap of wealth plundered from the great mountain, carries it town after town to those who have nothing, and hurries on to fill the land.
36.nuance: The simile makes the river's silt and gems a gift with recipients: it goes to those who lack, not to the land at large. உள்ளம் இல்லவர் is read as 'those without means'; it could also be heard as 'those without heart', which would turn the gift into a rebuke of the mean, and the reading is not certain.

37.reading: Having drunk the triple must of maddened elephants, bathed in honey and fine gold-dust, and rubbed along carrying red sandalwood, sweet fruit and the rest until they were worn, the flood went on its fine way.

38.reading: Sweeping up the forest as a king who has seized a city carries off its spoils, the flood with its swelling water reached the great long sea, so that one might ask whether it had come to besiege the sea's own land.
38.nuance: வீடு இல் பட்டினம் in line 1 is obscure: a city left without houses, or one with no escape; the king's plunder is clear, the qualifier is not.

39.reading: They say the river named Sarai, a maiden with broad warm breasts, came down with her roaring water to set on the head of the lord of the wave-beaten sea a garland of foam for him to enjoy.
39.nuance: The river is a bride going to her husband the sea; என்பவே presents the conceit as a saying. The name சரை is given without anything to tie it to a known river.

40.reading: The water spread like the fronds of a fruiting coconut, ran through the mortared sluice-heads built beforehand for it, and, its coming announced through the land with the deep-voiced drum, crowded into the fields with a sweet roar.
40.nuance: The flood is not only wild water: channels prepared in advance and a drum proclaiming its arrival make it an event the land is organized to receive.

41.reading: Like an unconquerable elephant caught in the hunt, its fury checked at dam after dam, the water sank low and filled the tanks, they say, deep beyond footing like the chastity of high-born women, and filled the other waters too.
41.nuance: நிறைந்தன ('filled') plays on நிறை, the self-containment the epics pair with chastity: the tank's fullness within its banks is the woman's virtue held within bounds. நிலைப் படா is read as 'beyond a footing, unfathomable'; it may instead mean 'not standing still', and the comparison turns on which.

42.reading: The clamour, the roar of the fierce water and the drums that a hundred thousand guards beat, gathering from every quarter, sounded, they say, like the sea roaring along with the rain-clouds.
42.event: Guards gathered along the banks beat drums against the flood.

43.reading: The oxen, loving each other like uncle and nephew and matched like Kaman and Saman together, with humps fed full on grass, keep to their herds and excel at their work.
43.nuance: Kama and his brother Saman give the image of a matched yoke. பூமனும் in line 3 is obscure and its sense is not fixed.

44.reading: Long herds of curve-horned male buffalo and close-horned bulls, with the ploughmen singing to them, rush into the fragrant fields together and scatter the shoals of spotted varal fish: a flood of ploughmen.
44.nuance: The verse ends on வெள்ளமே, turning the word just used for the river's flood onto the crowd of ploughmen: the human work continues the water's.
44.event: The ploughmen drive buffalo and bulls into the fields to plough, scattering the fish.

45.reading: In the worked fields they sow the bright sprouts of red paddy with folded hands, saying 'grow with vigour', pull the seedlings saying 'these are ready', and set them that same day, the field-women going in their bands as they are told.
45.nuance: The sower's தொழுது is a bow to the seed itself, a wish spoken to the crop; no god is named.
45.event: The farmers sow the paddy with a gesture of worship, and the field-women pull and transplant the seedlings.

46.reading: As the women press the seedlings in together, the mud marking their broad breasts, bright kayal fish leap out, and where milk ran on the ground as a cow fed her calf in the field, the fish thrash about in it.
46.event: The field-women transplant, and fish leap into milk spilled by a suckling calf.

47.reading: The fish, having tasted the milk, leap onto the lotuses of the field; the startled bees fly off and swarm onto the garlands that bangled fisherwomen stringing pearls have hung up, so that the bees already there flee.
47.nuance: 46 to 48 are one chain of startlement passed from creature to creature, as 31 was one chain of falling fruit.

48.reading: The fleeing bees brush the brows of the kuvalai, then fall on the jasmine buds that have burst open breathing pollen and embrace them, with the bright bees humming as if to say 'receive us as guests'.
48.nuance: The household virtue of receiving the guest is lent to flowers; the bees are the guests the opened buds take in.

49.reading: Because the boundless din of the transplanters sounds like the thunder of a young cloud, the peacocks cry out, and the troubled cuckoos fall silent and shrink into the flowering groves like women faint of heart, they say.

50.reading: Where the field-women pour out toddy with bangled hands, a young swan drinks itself drunk at the pool where the drinkers' leavings have gathered and dallies with a young heron, so that the peahen must bring it to its senses.
50.nuance: The drink of the labourers spills into the animal world as comedy. The last line, with பெடை மயில் தெருட்டும், is read as the peahen sobering the swan; whom she admonishes is not certain.

51.reading: The farmers of the cool fields refrain from weeding out the kuvalai because it is like eyes, and keep out of the lotus because it is like a bright face; such is the nature of these farmers.
51.nuance: Their restraint comes from the flowers' likeness to a beloved's eyes and face, not from any rule about harm. Line 3 (பண் எழுத்து இயல் படப் பரப்பி இட்டனர்) is obscure: something is spread out in the ordered way of musical notation, perhaps the seedlings in rows.

52.reading: The patiri bears pearl-like round buds and flowers, and when something is thrown at a leaping heron in the water, the birds rise screaming like the swelling waves of the cool sea.
52.nuance: Line 2 (ஒத்த பூ உடற்றிய நாவின் நாகினால்) is obscure, and who throws, and what, is not clear from the Tamil.

53.reading: The paddy, its ear forming within like a green snake carrying young, slowly holds the grain and brings it forth; at first it holds its head up like the wealth of base men, then, heavy with grain, it bows like people of tested learning.
53.nuance: The two halves of the simile are one plant at two ages: the stalk that stands erect while empty is the same that bows when full, so bowing is shown as what fullness does, not a separate virtue.

claims.claim: the learned bow while the wealth of the base holds its head high

links.note: Kural 17 states that the sea itself depends on the cloud returning what it took; verses 32 to 38 narrate that loop, from clouds grazing the sea to the flood reaching the sea again.
links.teaches: Read together, the couplet's abstract dependence becomes a full itinerary, and the epic's long description gains its shape: it is a circuit of giving back, not a string of pictures.

gains.a: a reason for its sea-to-sea ordering: the run enacts a return the couplet says the world depends on
gains.b: the intermediate stages the couplet skips: mountain, falls, sluices and fields through which the returned water passes

links.note: The Kural likens the wise man's wealth to water filling the village tank; the Cintamani likens the river's flood to the hand of a generous man carrying wealth to those who have nothing.
links.teaches: The tradition's image ran both ways, wealth explained by water and water by giving, and the epic adds movement and direction toward the needy, where the Kural's tank waits to be drawn from.

gains.a: a moral precedent that makes the river's simile a statement about how wealth should behave
gains.b: an active counterpart to its still tank: wealth that goes out town by town to the needy instead of waiting to be drawn

links.note: Kural 978 opposes greatness that bows to smallness that admires itself; the paddy simile sets the base man's erect wealth and the learned man's bow in one stalk at two ages.
links.teaches: The pair shows that the bow and the raised head can be stages of one thing rather than two kinds of people: what stands erect is empty, and the same stalk bows once it is full.

gains.a: a general maxim that its farm image is illustrating, which lifts the last verse of the chapter into a lesson
gains.b: a picture of how the change from pride to humility happens, by ripening, which the couplet's fixed opposition does not show

links.note: Kural 1033 says the ploughman alone lives on his own, while all others bow (தொழுது) to eat; in the Cintamani the sower himself bows (தொழுது) to the seed as he sows.
links.teaches: The ploughman whom the Kural sets above all bowing still bows, to the crop on which his independence rests, so his self-sufficiency is itself a dependence.

gains.a: a sense of why its farmers' gesture matters: they are the ones the Kural says need bow to no one
gains.b: a limit: the independence it praises rests on a seed the ploughman must greet with folded hands

links.note: Both epics walk through rich wet fields; the Silappathikaram's Jain nun warns that a careless step may hurt crab and snail, while the Cintamani's narrator delights as the ploughing herds scatter the fish.
links.teaches: The ahimsa scruple that a Jain nun in one epic applies to every footstep in the fields is absent from the Jain poet's own celebration of ploughing, so the epics keep that scruple for the ascetic and not for the land's prosperity.

source_issues: Several lines are obscure as printed and could not be fixed without commentary: 38 line 1 (வீடு இல் பட்டினம்), 43 line 3 (பூமனும்), 51 line 3, 52 line 2 (நாவின் நாகினால்).
